lines.narration: Up on the footbridge over the crossing, Sean asks Han how he ended up in Tokyo at all. Han answers sideways, the way he answers everything: you know those old westerns, where the cowboys make a run for the border? This is my Mexico. It is a joke with a confession inside it.

Because there's a lot of money, Sean guesses, and Han's reply is the thesis of the whole film in three sentences. I have money. Trust in character is what I need around me. One car in exchange for knowing what a man is made of.
What happens if I don't, Sean asks - and Han gives him the only rule he lives by. Life's simple. You make choices and you don't look back.
So if you don't drift to win, Sean asks, what do you drift for? You really wanna know? Okay, let's go - and the answer turns out not to be a sentence at all.
Two cars, one empty boulevard, and two women in the back seat.

The Skyline and the RX-7 lock into orbit around each other inside their own smoke, swapping lines for nothing - no finish line, no money, no crowd. That is the answer. Han drifts because for about forty seconds it is the only thing in his life he fully controls.
On a mountain pull-out the next morning the whole lesson is one instruction: out here, you drift by feeling. So feel it.

He runs the same clifftop hairpin again and again, harness-strapped, sawing at the wheel, sliding back into the pull-out in a cloud of his own dust. Every one of those runs costs a set of tyres he cannot pay for.

Meanwhile Boswell has no idea. Sean's father - the naval officer who took him in on condition he went to school and came straight home - lets himself into the flat and hits the light. Dark rooms, and a kitchen nobody has eaten in.
He parts the hanging coats, looks at a bed that has not been slept in, and stops pretending he does not know.
Upstairs at the garage rail, Reiko, who runs Han's floor, tells him someone is waiting below. It is Sean, back for more. The lessons are about to stop being lessons.

Han lets him off the leash: two cars door to door down a mountain road, then an empty expressway, then a concrete parking deck, pillar to pillar. Sean has stopped looking frightened, which matters, because next time there will be a debt and a crowd attached.

The crowd closes on his car in the neon plaza and he grins through the hands reaching in. Neela - the girl from his class - watches from the edge with a small smile she would not want anyone else to see.
Daylight, a classroom, and a chat window open on her laptop: bama boy, how come i never c u drift.

Over vending-machine noodles under a stacked highway overpass, he calls her a gaijin, and she stops him cold. She hates that word; it is what the other kids used on her. Outsider, she tells him, can mean a lot of things.

Then she gives him the whole thing in three sentences. Her mother came out from Australia straight after high school and went to work in a hostess bar; she died when Neela was ten; and the grandmother who took her in afterwards was DK's. Which means the Drift King who owns her is also the family that saved her.

So Sean gives her his: parents split when he was three, and after that he and his mother moved, and moved again, mostly because of him. No - all because of him. She is the first person in Tokyo who did not need that explained.

That night she drives. Up the hairpins with the city burning below, she tells him she has been coming here since before she had a licence. Cutting class, sneaking out, watching the older kids drift. It was different back then, she says. Nobody bothered them.
No past, no future, no problems, she finishes for him. Just a moment. Then he stops talking and watches her drive, and that is the second this becomes a problem for everybody.
Back at the dockside yard he asks Twinkie - the hustler from his class - for another set of tyres. Third set today, and sticky rubber is not cheap.

Morimoto, DK's enforcer, puts Sean face down on the concrete with one swing, and Han and the whole crew just watch - on yakuza turf, stepping in turns a beating into a war. Sean glares back instead of staying down - brave, and exactly the instinct that got him shipped out of Alabama.
Han's only comment: he didn't just play with fire, he soaked the matches in gasoline.

By morning he is shouldering through the school gates with his face still coming apart. Neela breaks off mid-conversation to look at him - which, in a city where DK decides who she talks to, is not a small thing to do in public.
So she does something worse. Still in her school uniform, she walks through the back of DK's club and stops in the doorway of the lounge. He is sitting with a boot on the table between two hostesses.
You've changed, DK, she says. Three words, in front of his men - and for someone whose whole position rests on never being contradicted, that is the one thing he cannot let go.
Then DK reaches for the only thing he knows will land: they say your mother was the best trick in all of Kabukicho. Leave my mother out of this, she tells him.

He backs her against a perforated wall and closes the gap until their faces almost touch, and she stops answering, turns her head aside and drops her eyes. It is the first time in this film anybody takes something off her, and he does it without once raising his voice, which is somehow worse than if he had.
